Could not the reverse occur with me? Or perhaps the meaning of what I said was that I had still a long and dangerous way to the throne. Who knows if the gods will allow me to accomplish it? And do not let me accomplish it, father of gods and men, if in the future thou seest in me a waster of the most precious gift which thou hast entrusted to me,--the blood of my subjects!

div.head: ARIDÄUS.
div.p: Yes, prince; what is a king, if he be not a father? What is a hero void of human love? Now I recognise this also in you, and am your friend again! But come, come; we must not remain alone here! We are too serious for one another. Follow me!

div.head: PHILOTAS.
div.p: Pardon, king----

div.head: ARIDÄUS.
div.p: Do not refuse!

div.head: PHILOTAS.
div.p: Thus, as I am, shall I show myself to many eyes?

div.head: ARIDÄUS.
div.p: Why not?

div.head: PHILOTAS.
div.p: I cannot, king, I cannot!

div.head: ARIDÄUS.
div.p: And the reason?

div.head: PHILOTAS.
div.p: O, the reason! It would make you laugh.

div.head: ARIDÄUS.
div.p: So much the better,--let me hear it! I am a human being, and like to laugh and cry.

div.head: PHILOTAS.
div.p: Well, laugh then! See, king, I have no sword, and should not like to appear amongst soldiers without this mark of the soldier.

div.head: ARIDÄUS.
div.p: My laughing turns to joy! I have thought of that beforehand, and your wish will be gratified at once. Strato has the order to get your sword again for you.

div.head: PHILOTAS.
div.p: Let us then await him here!

div.head: ARIDÄUS.
div.p: And then you will accompany me?

div.head: PHILOTAS.
div.p: Then I will follow you immediately.

div.head: ARIDÄUS.
div.p: As we willed it! There he comes! Well, Strato!
Strato (with a sword in his hand), Aridäus, Philotas.

div.head: STRATO.
div.p: King! I came to the soldier who had taken the prince and demanded the prince's sword from him in your name. But hear how nobly the soldier refused! "The king," he said, "must not take the sword from me! It is a good sword, and I shall use it in his service. I must also keep a remembrance of this deed. By the gods, it was none of my least! The prince is a young demon. But perhaps you wish only the precious hilt!" And on this, before I could prevent it, his strong hand had broken off the hilt, and throwing it contemptuously before my feet--"There it is," he continued, "what care I for your gold?"

div.head: ARIDÄUS.
div.p: O Strato, make good for me what this man has done!

div.head: STRATO.
div.p: I have done so. And here is one of your swords!

div.head: ARIDÄUS.
div.p: Give it me! Will you accept it, prince, instead of yours?

div.head: PHILOTAS.
div.p: Let me see! Ha! (aside.) Be thanked, ye gods! (eyeing it long and earnestly). A sword!

div.head: STRATO.
div.p: Have I not chosen well, prince?

div.head: ARIDÄUS.
div.p: What do you find in it so worthy of your deep attention?

div.head: PHILOTAS.
div.p: That it is a sword!--(recovering himself.) And a beautiful sword! I shall not lose anything by this exchange. A sword!

div.head: ARIDÄUS.
div.p: You tremble, prince!

div.head: PHILOTAS.
div.p: With joy! It seems, however, a trifle short for me. But why short? A step nearer to the enemy replaces what is wanting in the steel. Beloved sword! What a beautiful thing is a sword,--to play with and to use! I have never played with anything else.

div.head: ARIDÄUS (to Strato).
div.p: O the wondrous combination of child and hero!

div.head: PHILOTAS (aside).
div.p: Beloved sword! Could I but be alone with thee! But, courage!

div.head: ARIDÄUS.
div.p: Now gird on the sword, prince, and follow me!

div.head: PHILOTAS.
div.p: Directly! Yet one must not know one's friend and one's sword only outwardly (he draws it, and Strato steps between him and the king).

div.head: STRATO.
div.p: I understand the steel better than the workmanship. Believe me, prince, the steel is good. The king has cleft more than one helmet with it since his youth.

div.head: PHILOTAS.
div.p: I shall never grow so strong as that! But--Do not step so near, Strato!

div.head: STRATO.
div.p: Why not?

div.head: PHILOTAS.
div.p: So! (springing back and swinging the sword through the air). It has the right swing.

div.head: ARIDÄUS.
div.p: Prince, spare your wounded arm! You will excite yourself!

div.head: PHILOTAS.
div.p: Of what do you remind me, king? Of my misfortune--no, of my shame! I was wounded and made prisoner. Yes, but I shall never be so again! By this my sword, I shall never be so again! No, my father, no! To-day a wonder spares you the shameful ransom of your son; his death may spare it you in the future!--His certain death, when he shall see himself surrounded again! Surrounded again? Horrible! I am so! I am surrounded! What now? Companions! Friends! Brothers! Where are you? All dead? Enemies everywhere! Through here, Philotas! Ha! That is for you, rash fellow!--And that for you!--And that for you! (striking around him.)

div.head: STRATO.
div.p: Prince! what ails you? Calm yourself (approaches him.)

div.head: PHILOTAS (stepping away from him).
div.p: You too, Strato? You too? O, foe, be generous! Kill me! Do not make me captive! No, I do not deliver myself up! Were you all, who surround me, Stratos, yet I will defend myself against you all--against a world will I defend myself! Do your best, my foes! But you will not? You will not kill me, cruel men? You only wish to have me alive? I laugh at you! To take me prisoner alive? Me? Sooner shall this sword--this sword--shall pierce this breast--sooner--before--(he stabs himself.)

div.head: ARIDÄUS.
div.p: God! Strato!

div.head: STRATO.
div.p: King!

div.head: PHILOTAS.
div.p: I wished it thus! (sinking back.)

div.head: ARIDÄUS.
div.p: Hold him, Strato! Help! help for the prince! Prince, what raving anguish----

div.head: PHILOTAS.
div.p: Forgive me, king! I have dealt you a more deadly blow than myself! I die, and soon will peaceful lands enjoy the fruit of my death. Your son, king, is a prisoner, and the son of my father is free!

div.head: ARIDÄUS.
div.p: What do I hear?

div.head: STRATO.
div.p: Then it was your purpose, prince? But as our prisoner, you had no right over yourself!

div.head: PHILOTAS.
div.p: Do not say that, Strato! Should a man be able to fetter another's liberty to die, the liberty which the gods have left in all vicissitudes of life?

div.head: STRATO.
div.p: O king! Terror has paralyzed him! King!

div.head: ARIDÄUS.
div.p: Who calls me?

div.head: STRATO.
div.p: King!

div.head: ARIDÄUS.
div.p: Be silent!

div.head: STRATO.
div.p: The war is over, king!

div.head: ARIDÄUS.
div.p: Over? You lie, Strato! The war is not over, prince! Die! yes, die! But carry with you this tormenting thought! You believed, as a true ignorant boy, that fathers were all of one and the same mould,--all of the soft, effeminate nature of your father. They are not all like him! I am not so! What do I care about my son? And do you think that he cannot die as well for his father as you did for yours? Let him die! Let his death too spare me the disgraceful ransom! Strato, I am bereft now, I poor man! You have a son;--he shall be mine. For a son one must have! Happy Strato!

div.head: PHILOTAS.
div.p: Your son too lives still, king! And will live! I hear it!

div.head: ARIDÄUS.
div.p: Does he live still? Then I must have him back. But you--die! I will have him back, let what will come of it. And in exchange for you! Or I will have such disgrace and dishonour shown to your body--I will have it----

div.head: PHILOTAS.
div.p: The dead body!--If you will revenge yourself, king, awaken it again!

div.head: ARIDÄUS.
div.p: Ah! What do I say?

div.head: PHILOTAS.
div.p: I pity you! Farewell, Strato! There, where all virtuous friends and all brave men are members of one blessed state--in Elysium we shall meet again! We also, king, shall meet again.

div.head: ARIDÄUS.
div.p: And reconciled! Prince!

div.head: PHILOTAS.
div.p: O then, ye gods, receive my triumphant soul; and thou, goddess of peace, thy offering!

div.head: ARIDÄUS.
div.p: Hear me, prince!

div.head: STRATO.
div.p: He dies! Am I traitor, king, if I weep over your enemy? I cannot restrain myself. A wondrous youth!

lg.l: Weep over him, weep! And I too! Come! I must have my son again. But do not oppose me, if I pay too high a ransom for him! In vain have we shed our streams of blood, in vain have we conquered lands. There he departs with our booty, the greater victor!--Come! Get me my son! And when I have him, I will no more be king. Do ye believe, ye men, that one does not grow weary of it? (Exeunt.)

div.head: A TRAGEDY IN FIVE ACTS.
div.p: (Translated by B. Dillon Boylan.)

'Emilia Galotti' was commenced in 1757, when Lessing was at Leipzig, but was thrown aside for some years, until in 1767, when at Hamburg, he again took it up, intending to have it represented on the Hamburg stage. But on the failure of the theatrical enterprise with which he was connected, he once more abandoned it until 1771, when he again turned his attention to it, and completed it in February of the following year. It was immediately represented on the Brunswick stage.

div.head: DRAMATIS PERSONÆ.
div.p: Emilia Galotti.

Odoardo and
Claudia Galotti,
parents of Emilia.
Hettore Gonzaga, Prince of Guastalla.
Marinelli, the Prince's Chamberlain.
Camillo Rota, one of the Prince's Councillors.
Conti, an artist.
Count Appiani.
Angelo, a bandit.
Pirro and sundry servants.

div.head: Scene I.--The Prince's Cabinet.
div.p: The Prince, seated at a desk, which is covered with papers.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: Complaints; nothing but complaints! Petitions; nothing but petitions! Wretched employment! And yet we are envied! To be sure, if we could relieve every one, we might indeed be envied. Emilia? (opening a petition, and looking at the signature.) An Emilia? Yes--but an Emilia Bruneschi--not Galotti. Not Emilia Galotti. What does she want, this Emilia Bruneschi? (Reads) She asks much--too much. But her name is Emilia. It is granted (signs the paper, and rings).
Enter a Servant.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: Are any of the Councillors in the antechamber?

div.head: SERVANT.
div.p: No, your Highness.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: I have begun the day too early. The morning is so beautiful, I will take a drive. The Marquis Marinelli shall accompany me. Let him be called. (Exit Servant.) I can attend to nothing more. I was so happy--delightful thought! so happy--when all at once this wretched Bruneschi must be named Emilia. Now all my peace is fled.
Re-enter the Servant, bringing a note.

div.head: SERVANT.
div.p: The Marquis has been sent for; and here is a letter from the Countess Orsina.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: The Countess Orsina? Put it down.

div.head: SERVANT.
div.p: Her courier waits.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: I will send an answer if necessary. Where is she, in town, or at her villa?

div.head: SERVANT.
div.p: She arrived in town yesterday.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: So much the worse--the better, I mean. There is less reason for the messenger to wait. (Exit Servant.) My dear Countess! (with sarcasm, as he takes up the letter) as good as read (throwing it down again). Well, well, I fancied I loved her--one may fancy anything. It may be that I really did love her. But--I did.
Re-enter Servant.

div.head: SERVANT.
div.p: The painter Conti requests the honour----

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: Conti? Good! admit him. That will change the current of my thoughts (rising).
Conti, The Prince.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: Good morning, Conti. How goes it with you? How does art thrive?

div.head: CONTI.
div.p: Art is starving, Prince.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: That must not--shall not be, within the limits of my small dominions. But the artist must be willing to work.

div.head: CONTI.
div.p: Work! that is his happiness. But too much work may rain his claim to the title of artist.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: I do not mean that his works should be many, but his labour much: a little, but well done. But you do not come empty-handed, Conti?

div.head: CONTI.
div.p: I have brought the portrait which your Highness ordered; and another which you did not order; but as it is worthy of inspection----

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: That one, is it? And yet I do not well remember----

div.head: CONTI.
div.p: The Countess Orsina.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: True. The commission, however, was given rather long ago.

div.head: CONTI.
div.p: Our beauties are not every day at the artist's command. In three months, the Countess could only make up her mind to sit once.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: Where are the pictures?

div.head: CONTI.
div.p: In the antechamber. I will fetch them (exit).

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: Her portrait! Let it come; it is not herself. But perhaps I may see in the picture what I can no longer find in her person. But I have no wish to make such a discovery. The importunate painter! I almost believe that she has bribed him. But even were it so, if another picture which is pourtrayed in brighter colours and on a different canvas, could be obliterated to make room for her once more in my heart, I really think that I should be content. When I loved the Countess, I was ever gay, sprightly, and cheerful; now I am the reverse. But no, no, no; happy or unhappy, it is better as it is.
The Prince, Conti, with the portraits; he places one with the face reversed against a chair, and prepares to show the other.

div.head: CONTI.
div.p: I beg your Highness will bear in mind the limits of our art; much of the highest perfection of beauty lies altogether beyond its limits. Look at it in this position.

div.head: PRINCE (after a brief inspection).
div.p: Excellent! Conti, most excellent! It does credit to your taste,--to your skill. But flattered, Conti--quite, infinitely flattered!

div.head: CONTI.
div.p: The original did not seem to be of your opinion. But, in truth, she is not more flattered than art is bound to flatter. It is the province of art to paint as plastic nature--if there is such a thing--intended her original design, without the defects which the unmanageable materials render inevitable, and free from the ravages which result from a conflict with time.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: The intelligent artist has therefore double merit. But the original, you say, notwithstanding all this----

div.head: CONTI.
div.p: Pardon me, Prince! The original is a person who commands my respect. I did not intend to insinuate anything to her disadvantage.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: As much as you please. But what said the original?

div.head: CONTI.
div.p: "I am satisfied," said the Countess, "if I am not plainer."

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: Not plainer! The original herself!

div.head: CONTI.
div.p: And she uttered this with an expression of which the portrait affords no trace, no idea.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: That is just what I meant; therein lies your infinite flattery. Oh! I know well her proud, contemptuous look, which would disfigure the face of one of the Graces. I do not deny that a handsome mouth set off with a slight curl of scorn, sometimes acquires thereby additional beauty. But, observe, it must be only slight; the look must not amount to grimace, as it does with this Countess. The eyes, too, must keep control over the disdainful charmer; eyes which the worthy Countess decidedly does not possess. You do not even give them to her in the picture.

div.head: CONTI.
div.p: Your Highness, I am perfectly amazed.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: And wherefore? All that could be achieved by the resources of art out of the great prominent staring Medusa eyes of the Countess, you have honourably accomplished. Honourably, I say, but less honourably would have been more honest; for tell me yourself, Conti, is the character of the individual expressed by this picture? yet it should be. You have converted pride into dignity, disdain into a smile, and the gloom of discontent into soft melancholy.

div.head: CONTI (somewhat vexed).
div.p: Ah! Prince, we painters expect that a portrait when finished will find the lover as warm as when he ordered it. We paint with eyes of love, and the eyes of love alone must judge our works.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: 'Tis true, Conti; but why did you not bring it a month sooner? Lay it aside. What is the other?

div.head: CONTI (taking it up and holding it still reversed).
div.p: It is also a female portrait.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: Then I had almost rather not see it; for the ideal depicted here (pointing to his forehead), or rather here (laying his hand upon his heart), it cannot equal. I should like, Conti, to admire your art in other subjects.

div.head: CONTI.
div.p: There may be more admirable examples of art, but a more admirable subject than this cannot exist.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: Then I'll lay a wager, Conti, that it is the portrait of the artist's own mistress. (Conti turns the picture.) What do I see? Your work, Conti, or the work of my fancy? Emilia Galotti!

div.head: CONTI.
div.p: How, Prince! do you know this angel?

div.head: PRINCE (endeavouring to compose himself, but unable to remove his eyes from the picture).
div.p: A little; just enough to recognise her. A few weeks ago I met her with her mother at an assembly; since then I have only seen her in sacred places, where staring is unseemly. I know her father also; he is not my friend. He it was who most violently opposed my pretensions to Sabionetta. He is a veteran, proud and unpolished, but upright and brave.

div.head: CONTI.
div.p: You speak of the father, this is the daughter.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: By Heavens! you must have stolen the resemblance from her mirror (with his eyes still rivetted on the picture). Oh, you well know, Conti, that we praise the artist most when we forget his merits in his works.

div.head: CONTI.
div.p: Yet I am extremely dissatisfied with this portrait, and nevertheless I am satisfied with being dissatisfied with myself. Alas! that we cannot paint directly with our eyes! On the long journey from the eye through the arm to the pencil, how much is lost! But, as I have already said, though I know what is lost, and how and why it is lost, I am as proud and prouder of this loss than of what I have preserved. For by the former I perceive more than by the latter, that I am a good painter, though my hand is not always so. Or do you hold, Prince, that Raffaelle would not have been the greatest of all artists even had he unfortunately been born without hands?

div.head: PRINCE (turning his eyes a moment from the picture).
div.p: What do you say, Conti? What was your enquiry?

div.head: CONTI.
div.p: Oh, nothing--nothing; mere idle observations! Your soul, I observe, was wholly in your eyes. I like such souls and such eyes.

div.head: PRINCE (affecting coldness).
div.p: And so, Conti, you really consider Emilia Galotti amongst the first beauties of our city.

div.head: CONTI.
div.p: Amongst them? Amongst the first? The first of our city? You jest, Prince, or your eyesight must have been all this time as insensible as your hearing.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: Dear Conti (again fixing his eyes on the picture), how can we uninitiated trust our eyes? In fact, none but an artist can judge of beauty.

div.head: CONTI.
div.p: And must the feeling of every person wait for the decision of a painter? To a cloister with him who would learn from us what is beautiful! But this much I must own to you, as a painter, Prince. It is one of the greatest delights of my life that Emilia Galotti has sat to me. This head, this countenance, this forehead, these eyes, this nose, this mouth, this chin, this neck, this bosom, this shape, this whole form, are from the present time forward my only model of female beauty. The original picture for which she sat, is in the possession of her absent father. But this copy----

div.head: PRINCE (turning to him quickly).
div.p: Well, Conti--is not surely bespoke already?

div.head: CONTI.
div.p: Is for you, Prince, if it affords you any pleasure.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: Pleasure! (smiling.) How can I do better than make your model of female beauty my own? There, take back that other portrait, and order a frame for it.

div.head: CONTI.
div.p: Good.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: As rich and splendid as the carver can possibly make it. It shall be placed in the gallery. But this must remain here. A study need not be treated with so much ceremony; one does not hang it up for display. It should always be at hand. I thank you, Conti, cordially. And as I said before, the arts shall never starve in my dominions, as long as I have bread. Send to my treasurer, Conti, and let him pay your own price for both pictures; as much as you please, Conti.

div.head: CONTI.
div.p: I must begin to fear, Prince, that you mean to reward me for something else besides my art?

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: Oh the jealousy of an artist! No, no! But remember, Conti, as much as you please. (Exit Conti.)
The Prince.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: Yes, as much as he pleases. (Turning to the picture.) Thou art mine, too cheap at any price. Oh, thou enchanting work of art! Do I then possess thee? But who shall possess thyself, thou still more beautiful masterpiece of nature? Claim what you will, honest old mother; ask what you will, morose old father. Demand any price. Yet, dear enchantress, I should be far more happy to buy thee from thyself! This eye! how full of love and modesty! This mouth! when it speaks, when it smiles! This mouth!--Some one comes.--I am still too jealous of thee. (Turning the picture to the wall.) It is Marinelli. I wish I had not sent for him! What a morning might I have had!
Marinelli, The Prince.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: Your Highness will pardon me; I was not prepared for so early a summons.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: I felt an inclination to drive out, the morning was so fine. But now it is almost over, and my inclination has subsided. (After a short pause). Any news, Marinelli?

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: Nothing of importance that I know. The Countess Orsina arrived in town yesterday.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: Yes, here lies her morning salutation (pointing to the letter), or whatever it may be. I am not inquisitive about it. Have you seen her?

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: Am I not unfortunately her confidant? But if ever I am so again with a lady who takes it into her head to love you desperately, Prince, may I----

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: No rash vows, Marinelli.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: Indeed, Prince! Is it possible? The Countess, then, is not so utterly mistaken.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: Quite mistaken, certainly. My approaching union with the Princess of Massa compels me in the first place to break off all such connections.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: If that were all, the Countess would doubtless know as well how to submit to her fate, as the Prince to his.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: My fate is harder far than hers. My heart is sacrificed to a miserable political consideration. She has but to take back hers, and need not bestow it against her inclination.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: Take it back! "Why take it back," asks the Countess, "for a wife, whom policy and not love attaches to the Prince?" With a wife of that kind the mistress may still hold her place. It is not, therefore, for a wife that she dreads being sacrificed, but----

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: Perhaps another mistress. What then? would you make a crime of that, Marinelli?

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: I, Prince? Oh, confound me not with the foolish woman whose cause I advocate--from pity! For yesterday I own she greatly moved me. She wished not to mention her attachment to you, and strove to appear cold and tranquil. But in the midst of the most indifferent topics, some expression, some allusion, escaped her, which betrayed her tortured heart. With the most cheerful demeanour she said the most melancholy things, and on the other hand uttered the most laughable jests with an air of deep distress. She has taken to books for refuge, which I fear will be her ruin.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: Yes, for books gave the first blow to her poor understanding. And, Marinelli, you will scarcely employ for the purpose of renewing my attachment, that which was the chief cause of our separation. If love renders her foolish, she would sooner or later have become so, even without such influence. But enough of her! To something else. Is there nothing new in town?

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: Next to nothing; for that Count Appiani will be married to-day is little better than nothing.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: Count Appiani! To whom? I have not heard that he is engaged.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: The affair has been kept a profound secret. And indeed, there was not much to create a sensation. You will smile, Prince; but it ever happens so with sentimental youths! Love always plays the worst of tricks. A girl without fortune or rank has managed to catch him in her snares, without any trouble, but with a little display of virtue, sensibility, wit, and so forth.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: The man who can wholly resign himself to the impressions which innocence and beauty make upon him is, in my opinion, rather to be envied than derided. And what is the name of the happy fair one? For though I well know, Marinelli, that you and Appiani dislike each other, he is nevertheless a very worthy young man, a handsome man, a rich man, and an honourable man. I should like to be able to attach him to myself.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: If it be not too late; for, as far as I can learn, it is not his intention to seek his fortune at court. He will retire with his spouse to his native valleys of Piedmont, and indulge himself in hunting chamois or training marmots upon the Alps. What can he do better? Here his prospects are blighted by the connection he has formed. The first circles are closed against him.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: The first circles! What are they worth, mere resorts of ceremony, restraint, ennui, and poverty? But how call you the fair being who is the cause of all these wondrous sacrifices?

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: A certain--Emilia Galotti?

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: What! Marinelli! a certain----

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: Emilia Calotti.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: Emilia Galotti? Never!----

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: Assuredly, your Highness.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: But no, I say. It is not, and it cannot be! You mistake the name. The family of Galotti is numerous. It may be a Galotti, but not Emilia Galotti!

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: Emilia--Emilia Galotti.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: There must be another who bears the same names. You said, however, a certain Emilia Galotti,--a certain one. Of the real Emilia, none but a fool could so speak.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: Your Highness is excited. Do you know this Emilia?

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: It is my place to question, not yours, Marinelli. Is she the daughter of Colonel Galotti, who resides at Sabionetta?

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: The same.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: Who lives here in Guastalla with her mother.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: The same.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: Near the church of All-Saints.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: The same.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: In a word (turning hastily to the portrait, and giving it to Marinelli)--there! is it this Emilia Galotti? Pronounce again those damning words, "the same," and plunge a dagger in my heart.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: The same.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: Traitor! This? this Emilia Galotti--will to-day be----

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: The Countess Appiani. (The Prince seizes the portrait from the hands of Marinelli, and flings it aside.)--The marriage will be celebrated privately at her father's villa, in Sabionetta. About noon the mother and daughter, the Count, and perhaps a few friends, will leave town together.

div.head: PRINCE (throwing himself in a state of desperation into a chair).
div.p: Then I am lost, and care no more for life.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: What thus affects your Highness?

div.head: PRINCE (starting towards him again).
div.p: Traitor! what affects me thus? Yes, in truth, I love her! I adore her! You may, perhaps, know it, may even long have known it; all of you who desire that I should wear for ever the ignominious fetters of the proud Orsina. That you, Marinelli, who have so often assured me of your sincere friendship--but a Prince has no friend, can have no friend--that you should act so treacherously, so deceitfully, as to conceal till this moment the peril which threatened my love.--Oh, if ever I forgive you this, let no sin of mine be pardoned!

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: I could scarcely find words, Prince, to express my astonishment--even if you gave me the opportunity. You love Emilia Galotti? Hear, then, my oath in reply to yours. If I have ever known or suspected this attachment in the slightest degree, may the angels and saints abandon me! I repeat the same imprecation for Orsina. Her suspicions were directed to a wholly different quarter.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: Pardon me, then, Marinelli (throwing himself into his arms), and pity me.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: Well, yes, Prince. There see the consequence of your reserve. "A prince has no friends." And why? Because he will have none. To-day you honour us with your confidence, entrust to us your most secret wishes, open your whole soul to us--and to-morrow we are as perfect strangers to you, as if you had never exchanged a word with us.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: Alas, Marinelli, how could I entrust a secret to you which I would scarcely confess to myself?

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: And, which you have, therefore, of course, not confessed to the author of your uneasiness?

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: To her!--All my endeavours have been fruitless to speak with her a second time.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: And the first time----

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: I spoke to her;--Oh, my brain is turned, and must I continue this conversation longer? You behold me at the mercy of the waves, and why inquire how all this has happened? Save me if you can, and then question me.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: Save you! Is there much to save? What your Highness has not confessed to Emilia Galotti, you will confess to the Countess Appiani. Goods which cannot be obtained in their primitive perfection, must be bought at second hand, and are often, on that account, bought at a cheaper rate.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: Be serious, Marinelli, or----

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: To be sure, such articles are generally so much the worse----

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: For shame, Marinelli.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: And the Count intends to leave this country too. Well, we must devise some scheme----

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: And what scheme? My best and dearest Marinelli, contrive something for me. What would you do, were you in my situation?

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: Above all things, I should regard a trifle as a trifle--and say to myself that I would not be what I am for nothing--your Highness!

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: Delude me not with a power of which I can, on this occasion, make no use. To-day, said you?--This very day?

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: To-day it is to take place;--but it is only things which have taken place that cannot be recalled. (After a short pause.) Prince, will you let me act as I please? Will you approve all I do?

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: Anything, Marinelli, which can avert this blow.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: Then let us lose no time. You must not remain in town, but go to your palace at Dosalo. The road to Sabionetta passes it. Should I not succeed in removing the Count, I think--yes, yes, he will be caught in that snare without doubt. You wish to send an ambassador to Massa respecting your marriage. Let the Count be ambassador, and order him to depart this very day.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: Excellent!--Bring him to my palace.--Haste, haste!--I will leave town instantly. (Exit Marinelli.)

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: Instantly, instantly. Where is it? (Turns to the portrait) On the ground! That was too bad. (Takes it up) But look! And yet I will look at thee no more now. Why should I plunge the arrow deeper into the wound? (Lays it on the table). I have suffered and sighed long enough--longer than I ought, but done nothing, and my listless inactivity had nearly ruined all.--And may not all yet be lost? May not Marinelli fail? Why should I rely on him alone?--It occurs to me that at this hour (looks at his watch) at this very hour, the pious girl daily attends mass at the church of the Dominicans. How, if I attempted to address her there? But to-day--the day of her marriage--her heart will be occupied with other things than mass. Yet, who knows?--'tis but a step--(rings, and whilst he hastily arranges the papers on the table)--
Enter Servant.
My carriage!--Have none of the council arrived?

div.head: SERVANT.
div.p: Camillo Rota waits without.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: Admit him. (Exit Servant). But he must not attempt to detain me long. Not now--another time, I will attend to his scrupulous investigations----There was a petition of one Emilia Bruneschi--here it is--but, good Bruneschi, if your intercessor----
Enter Camillo Rota.
Come, Rota, come. There lie the papers which I have opened this morning--not very consoling--you will see what is to be done. Take them with you.

div.head: CAMILLO.
div.p: I will attend to them.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: Here is a petition from one Emilia Galot--I mean Bruneschi. I have already signed my consent to it--but yet the request is no trifle. You may defer the execution of it--or not--as you please.

div.head: CAMILLO.
div.p: Not as I please, your Highness.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: What more is there--anything to sign?

div.head: CAMILLO.
div.p: Sentence of death for your Highness's signature.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: With all my heart!--Where is it? Quick!

div.head: CAMILLO (starts and gazes at the Prince).
div.p: I said a death--warrant.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: I understood you plain enough. It might have been done by this. I am in haste.

div.head: CAMILLO (looking at his papers).
div.p: I really believe I have not brought it. I beg your Highness's forgiveness. It can be deferred till to-morrow.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: Be it so. Just collect these papers together. I must away. The rest to-morrow, Rota.

div.head: CAMILLO (shaking his head, as he collects the papers).
div.p: "With all my heart!"--A death-warrant, with all my heart! I would not have let him sign at such a moment, had the criminal murdered my own son.--"With all my heart!" "With all my heart"--The cruel words pierce my very soul. (Exit.)

div.head: Scene I.--A room in Galotti's house.
div.p: Claudia Galotti, Pirro.

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: Who dismounted just now in the court-yard? Pirro.

div.head: PIRRO.
div.p: My master, madam.

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: My husband? Is it possible?

div.head: PIRRO.
div.p: Here he comes.

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: So unexpectedly? (hastens towards him). My dearest lord!
Odoardo, and the foregoing.

div.head: ODOARDO.
div.p: Good morning, my love. Does not my arrival surprise you?

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: Most agreeably. But is it intended as no more than a surprise?

div.head: ODOARDO.
div.p: No more. Be not alarmed. The happiness of to-day awakened me early. The morning was so fine, and the ride so short, I fancied you would be so busy here to-day, and thought you might perhaps forget something: in a word, I am come to see you, and shall return immediately. Where is Emilia? Occupied with her dress, I have no doubt?

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: With her soul. She is gone to hear mass. "I have need," she said, "to-day more than at any other time to implore a blessing from above;" then leaving all else she took her veil, and disappeared.

div.head: ODOARDO.
div.p: Alone!

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: It is but a few steps----

div.head: ODOARDO.
div.p: One incautious step often leads to mischief.

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: Be not angry; but come in and rest a moment, and, if you please, take some refreshment.

div.head: ODOARDO.
div.p: Well, well, as you like. But she ought not to have gone alone.

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: Stay here, Pirro, in the antechamber, and excuse me to all visitors. (Exeunt Odoardo and Claudia.)
Pirro, and afterwards Angelo.

div.head: PIRRO.
div.p: All inquisitive visitors. How I have been questioned! Who comes here? (Enter Angelo, in a short mantle, with which he conceals his face.)

div.head: ANGELO.
div.p: Pirro! Pirro!

div.head: PIRRO.
div.p: An acquaintance, it seems. (Angelo throws back the mantle). Heavens! Angelo. You!

div.head: ANGELO.
div.p: Yes, Angelo, as you perceive. I have been wandering long enough round the house, in order to speak to you. One word with you----

div.head: PIRRO.
div.p: And dare you again appear in public? Don't you know that, in consequence of your last murder, you are declared an outlaw, a price has been put upon your head?

div.head: ANGELO.
div.p: You don't intend to claim it, I presume?

div.head: PIRRO.
div.p: What do you want? I implore you not to involve me in misfortune.

div.head: ANGELO.
div.p: In this way, you mean? (Showing a purse). Take it; it belongs to you.

div.head: PIRRO.
div.p: To me?

div.head: ANGELO.
div.p: Have you forgotten? The German gentleman, your last master----

div.head: PIRRO.
div.p: Hush!

div.head: ANGELO.
div.p: ----Whom you led into our clutches on the road to Pisa----

div.head: PIRRO.
div.p: If any one should overhear us!

div.head: ANGELO.
div.p: ----Had the kindness, you know, to bequeath us a valuable ring. Do you not remember? It was so valuable that we could not immediately convert it into money without suspicion. At length, however, I succeeded. I received a hundred pistoles for it, and this is your share. Take it.

div.head: PIRRO.
div.p: No, no! You may keep it.

div.head: ANGELO.
div.p: Well, with all my heart! If you don't care at what price you put your head in the market.

div.head: PIRRO.
div.p: Give it me, then (takes it). And now, what do you want? for I suppose you did not come in search of me merely for that purpose.

div.head: ANGELO.
div.p: It seems to you not very credible. Rascal! what do you think of us? That we are capable of withholding any man's earnings? That may be the way with honest people; but we don't follow their fashions. Farewell! (Affects to be going, but turns at the door). One question I must ask. Old Galotti has just come hurriedly into town quite alone. What does he want?

div.head: PIRRO.
div.p: Nothing, merely a ride. His daughter is to be married this evening, at his country house, whence he has come to Count Appiani. He awaits the moment with impatience.

div.head: ANGELO.
div.p: Then he will return soon?

div.head: PIRRO.
div.p: So soon, that if you remain any longer he will discover you. But you surely have no thoughts of attacking him. Take care. He is a man----

div.head: ANGELO.
div.p: Don't I know him? Have I not served under him in the army; but nevertheless if one could only get much from him! At what time do the young people follow him?

div.head: PIRRO.
div.p: Towards noon.

div.head: ANGELO.
div.p: With many attendants?

div.head: PIRRO.
div.p: A single carriage will contain the party--the mother, the daughter, and the count. A few friends from Sabionetta attend as witnesses.

div.head: ANGELO.
div.p: And the servants?

div.head: PIRRO.
div.p: Only two besides myself. I shall ride before.

div.head: ANGELO.
div.p: Good. Another question. Is the carriage Galotti's or the Count's?

div.head: PIRRO.
div.p: The Count's.

div.head: ANGELO.
div.p: That is unlucky. There is another outrider, besides a courageous driver. However----

div.head: PIRRO.
div.p: I am amazed. What do you intend? The few ornaments which the bride has will scarcely reward your trouble.

div.head: ANGELO.
div.p: Then the bride herself shall be the reward.

div.head: PIRRO.
div.p: And you mean that I should be your accomplice in this crime?

div.head: ANGELO.
div.p: You ride before! Then ride, ride, and take no trouble about the matter.

div.head: PIRRO.
div.p: Never!

div.head: ANGELO.
div.p: What?--I believe the fellow means to play the conscientious--you rascal! I think you know me. If you utter a syllable--if every circumstance be not as you have described it----

div.head: PIRRO.
div.p: But, Angelo, for Heaven's sake----

div.head: ANGELO.
div.p: Do what you cannot avoid. (Exit.)

div.head: PIRRO.
div.p: Ha! let the devil hold thee by a single hair, and thou art his for ever! Wretch that I am!
Odoardo and Claudia Galotti, Pirro.

div.head: ODOARDO.
div.p: She stays too long.

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: One moment more, Odoardo. It would distress her to miss seeing you.

div.head: ODOARDO.
div.p: I must wait upon the Count, too. How eager am I to call this worthy man my son! His conduct enchants me, and, above everything, his resolution to pass his days in his native valleys.

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: My heart almost breaks when I think of it. Must we so entirely lose our dear and only child!

div.head: ODOARDO.
div.p: Can you think you have lost her, when you know she is in the arms of an affectionate husband? Does not her happiness make your delight? You almost make me again suspect that your motive for remaining with her in town, far from an affectionate husband and father, was the bustle and the dissipation of the world, and proximity of the court, rather than the necessity of giving our daughter a proper education.

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: How unjust, Odoardo! But to-day, I may be allowed to speak somewhat in favour of town and court, though both are so hateful to your strict virtue; for here alone could love have united a couple formed for each other; here alone could the Count have found our Emilia, and he has found her.

div.head: ODOARDO.
div.p: That I allow. But were you right, good Claudia, because the result has been fortunate? It is well that this court education has ended so happily. Let us not affect to be wise, when we have only been fortunate. It is well that it has ended so happily. They who were destined for each other have found each other. Now let them go where peace and innocence invite them. Why should the Count remain here? To cringe--to fawn--to flatter--to supplant the Marinellis--to make a fortune which he does not want--to obtain a dignity, which he does not value?--Pirro!

div.head: PIRRO.
div.p: Sir!

div.head: ODOARDO.
div.p: Lead my horse to the Count's door. I'll follow you anon, and mount it there. (Exit Pirro).--Why should the Count serve here, when he may command elsewhere? Besides, you do not consider, Claudia, that, by his union with my daughter, he is utterly ruined with the Prince? The Prince hates me----

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: Less, perhaps, than you fear.

div.head: ODOARDO.
div.p: Fear! Should I fear anything so contemptible?

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: Why, have I not already told you that the Prince has seen our daughter?

div.head: ODOARDO.
div.p: The Prince! Where?

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: At the last assembly of the Chancellor Grimaldi, which he honoured with his presence. He conducted himself so graciously towards her----

div.head: ODOARDO.
div.p: Graciously?

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: Yes. He conversed with her for some time.

div.head: ODOARDO.
div.p: Conversed with her?

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: Appeared to be so delighted with her cheerfulness and good sense----

div.head: ODOARDO.
div.p: Delighted?

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: Spoke of her elegance and beauty, in terms of such admiration----

div.head: ODOARDO.
div.p: Admiration? And all this you relate to me in a tone of rapture. Oh, Claudia! vain, foolish mother!

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: Why so?

div.head: ODOARDO.
div.p: Well, well. This, too, has ended happily.--Ha! when I think----That were exactly the point where a wound would be to me most deadly.--A libertine, who admires, and seduces----Claudia! Claudia! The very thought rouses my fury. You ought to have mentioned this to me immediately.--But to-day I would not willingly say anything to vex you. And I should (as she takes him by the hand), were I to stay longer. Therefore, let me begone. God be with you, Claudia; follow me in safety. (Exit.)
Claudia, Galotti.

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: What a man! What rigid virtue--if virtue that should be called, to which everything seems suspicious and culpable. If this be a knowledge of mankind, who would not wish to remain in ignorance? Why does Emilia stay so long?----He dislikes the father--consequently, if he admire the daughter, he must mean to bring disgrace upon him!
Emilia and Claudia Galotti.

div.head: EMILIA (rushing in, much alarmed.)
div.p: Heaven be praised! I am now in safety. Or has he even followed me hither? (Throwing back her veil and espying her mother). Has he, my mother, has he?--No, thank Heaven.

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: What has happened to you, my daughter?

div.head: EMILIA.
div.p: Nothing--nothing.

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: And yet you look wildly round, and tremble in every limb!

div.head: EMILIA.
div.p: What have I had to hear?--And where have I been forced to hear it?

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: I thought you were at church.

div.head: EMILIA.
div.p: I was. But what are churches and altars to the vicious?--Oh, my mother! (Throws herself into Claudia's arms.)

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: Speak, my daughter, and remove my fears. What evil can have happened to you in so holy a place?

div.head: EMILIA.
div.p: Never should my devotion have been more fervent and sincere than on this day. Never was it less what it ought to have been.

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: Emilia we are all human. The faculty of praying fervently is not always in our power; but, in the eye of Heaven, the wish to pray is accepted as prayer.

div.head: EMILIA.
div.p: And our wish to sin as sin.

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: That my Emilia never wished.

div.head: EMILIA.
div.p: No, my mother. The grace of Heaven has preserved me from falling so low. But, alas! that the vice of others should render us accomplices in vice against our will!

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: Compose yourself.--Collect your thoughts as well as you can. Tell me at once what has happened to you.

div.head: EMILIA.
div.p: I had just sunk upon my knees, further from the altar than usual--for I arrived too late. I had just begun to raise my thoughts towards Heaven--when some person placed himself behind me--so close behind me! I could neither move forwards nor aside, however much I desired it, in my fear lest the devotion of my neighbour might interrupt my prayers. Devotion was the worst thing which I suspected. But it was not long before I heard a deep sigh close to my ear, and not the name of a saint;--no--the name--do not be angry, dear mother--the name of your daughter.--My own name! Oh, that a peal of thunder had at that moment made me deaf to the rest. The voice spoke of beauty and of love--complained that this day, which crowned my happiness (if such should prove the case) sealed his misery for ever. He conjured me--all this I was obliged to hear, but I did not look round. I wished to seem as if I was not listening. What more could I do? Nothing but pray that my guardian angel would strike me with deafness--even with eternal deafness. This was my prayer--the only prayer which I could utter. At length it was time to rise; the service came to an end. I trembled at the idea of being obliged to turn round--trembled at the idea of beholding him whose impiety had so much shocked me--and when I turned--when I beheld him----

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: Whom, my daughter?

div.head: EMILIA.
div.p: Guess, dear mother, guess: I thought I should have sunk into the earth. Himself!

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: Whom do you mean?

div.head: EMILIA.
div.p: The Prince!

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: The Prince! Blest be your father's impatience! He was here just now, and would not stay till you returned.

div.head: EMILIA.
div.p: My father here--and not stay till I returned!

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: If, in the midst of your confusion, you had told him too.

div.head: EMILIA.
div.p: Well, dear mother--could he have found anything in my conduct deserving of censure?

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: No--as little as in mine. And yet, yet--you do not know your father. When enraged, he would have mistaken the innocent for the guilty--in his anger he would have fancied me the cause of what I could neither prevent nor foresee. But proceed, my daughter, proceed. When you recognised the Prince, I trust that you were sufficiently composed to convince him by your looks, of the contempt which he deserved.

div.head: EMILIA.
div.p: That I was not. After the glance by which I recognised him, I had not courage to cast a second. I fled.

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: And the Prince followed you?

div.head: EMILIA.
div.p: I did not know it till I had reached the porch, where I felt my hand seized--by him. Shame compelled me to stop; as an effort to extricate myself would have attracted the attention of every one who was passing. This was the only reflection of which I was capable, or which I at present remember. He spoke, and I replied--but what he said, or what I replied, I know not.--Should I recollect it, my dear mother, you shall hear it. At present I remember nothing further. My senses had forsaken me.--In vain do I endeavour to recollect how I got away from him, and escaped from the porch. I found myself in the street--I heard his steps behind me--I heard him follow me into the house, and pursue me up the stairs----

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: Fear has its peculiar faculty, my daughter. Never shall I forget the look with which you rushed into this room!--No. He dared not follow you so far.--Heavens! had your father known this!--How angry was he when I merely told him that the Prince had lately beheld you with admiration! Be at ease, however, my dear girl. Fancy what has happened to be a mere dream. The result will be less, even, than a dream. You will be assured to-day from all similar designs.

div.head: EMILIA.
div.p: No, mother! The Count must know it--to him I must relate it.

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: Not for the world. Wherefore? Why? Do you wish to make him uneasy without a cause? And granting that he may not become so at present--know, my child, the poison which does not operate immediately, is not on that account less dangerous. That which has no effect upon the lover, may produce a serious one upon the husband. The lover might even be flattered at winning the prize from so great a rival; but when he has won it--alas, my dear Emilia, the lover often becomes quite another being. Heaven preserve you from such experience!

div.head: EMILIA.
div.p: You know, dear mother, how willingly I ever submit to your superior judgment. But should he learn from another that the Prince spoke to me to-day, would not my silence sooner or later increase his uneasiness?--I think it would be better not to conceal anything from him.

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: Weakness--a fond weakness. No, on no account, my daughter! Tell him nothing. Let him observe nothing.

div.head: EMILIA.
div.p: I submit. I have no will, dear mother, opposed to yours. Ah! (sighing deeply), I shall soon be well again. What a silly, timid thing I am! am I not, mother? I might have conducted myself otherwise, and should, perhaps, have compromised myself just a little.

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: I would not say this, my daughter, till your own good sense had spoken, which I was sure would be as soon as your alarm was at an end. The Prince is a gallant. You are too little used to the unmeaning language of gallantry. In your mind a civility becomes an emotion--a compliment, a declaration--an idea, a wish--a wish, a design. A mere nothing, in this language, sounds like everything, while everything is in reality nothing.

div.head: EMILIA.
div.p: Dear mother, my terror cannot but appear ridiculous to myself now. But my kind Appiani shall know nothing of it. He might, perhaps, think me more vain than virtuous----Ah! there he comes himself. That is his step.
Enter Appiani, in deep meditation. His eyes are cast down, and he approaches without observing Claudia and Emilia, till the latter runs towards him.

div.head: APPIANI.
div.p: Ha! My dearest! I did not expect to find you in the ante-room.

div.head: EMILIA.
div.p: I wish you to be cheerful, even where you do not expect to see me. Why so grave and solemn? Should not this day inspire joyful emotions?

div.head: APPIANI.
div.p: It is of greater value to me than my whole life; but it teems with so much bliss for me--perhaps it is this very bliss which makes me so grave--so solemn, as you express it (espies Claudia). Ha! You too here, dear madam. This day I hope to address you by a more familiar name.

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: Which will be my greatest pride.--How happy you are, Emilia! Why would not your father share our delight?

div.head: APPIANI.
div.p: But a few minutes have elapsed since I tore myself from his arms--or rather he from mine.--What a man your father is, my Emilia! A pattern of every manly virtue! With what sentiments does his presence inspire my soul! Never is my resolution to continue just and good, so firm as when I see or think of him. And by what, but by fulfilling this resolution, can I make myself worthy of the honour to be called his son--to become your husband, dear Emilia?

div.head: EMILIA.
div.p: And he would not wait for me!

div.head: APPIANI.
div.p: Because, in my opinion, this brief interview with his Emilia would have distressed him too much, too deeply affected his soul.

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: He expected to find you busy with your bridal ornaments, and heard----

div.head: APPIANI.
div.p: What I have learnt from him with the tenderest admiration. Right, my Emilia. I shall be blessed with a pious wife--and one who is not proud of her piety.

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: But let us not, whilst we attend to one subject, forget another. It is high time, Emilia. Go!

div.head: APPIANI.
div.p: Go! Why?

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: Surely, my lord, you would not lead her to the altar in her present attire.

div.head: APPIANI.
div.p: In truth, I was not, till you spoke, aware of that. Who can behold Emilia, and take heed of her dress? Yet why should I not lead her to the altar thus?

div.head: EMILIA.
div.p: No, dear Count, not exactly thus; yet in a dress not much more gay. In a moment I shall be ready. I do not mean to wear those costly jewels, which were the last present of your prodigal generosity, no, nor anything suited to such jewels. Oh, I could quarrel with those jewels were they not your present--for thrice I've dreamt----

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: Indeed! I know nothing of that.

div.head: EMILIA.
div.p: That while I wore them, every diamond changed suddenly to a pearl--and pearls, you know, dear mother, signify tears.

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: Child, the interpretation is more visionary than the dream. Were you not always more fond of pearls than diamonds?

div.head: EMILIA.
div.p: I assuredly, dear mother--assuredly----

div.head: APPIANI (thoughtful and melancholy).
div.p: Signify tears!

div.head: EMILIA.
div.p: How! Does that affect you? You?

div.head: APPIANI.
div.p: It does, though I ought to be ashamed that such is the case; yet when the fancy is once disposed to sad impressions----

div.head: EMILIA.
div.p: But why should yours be so? Guess the subject of my thoughts. What did I wear, and how did I look when I first attracted your attention? Do you remember?

div.head: APPIANI.
div.p: Remember! I never see you in idea but in that dress, and I see you so, even when you are not thus attired.

div.head: EMILIA.
div.p: I mean to wear one of the same colour and form--flowing and loose.

div.head: APPIANI.
div.p: Excellent!

div.head: EMILIA.
div.p: And my hair----

div.head: APPIANI.
div.p: In its own dark beauty, in curls formed by the hand of nature.

div.head: EMILIA.
div.p: Not forgetting the rose. Right! Have a little patience, and you shall see me thus. (Exit.)
Count Appiani, Claudia Galotti.

div.head: APPIANI (looks after her with a downcast mien).
div.p: "Pearls signify tears!"--a little patience! Yes! if we could but defy time! If a minute on the clock were not sometimes an age within us!

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: Emilia's remark was no less just than quick, Count. You are to-day more grave than usual. And yet you are but a step from the object of your wishes. Do you repent that you have attained the wished-for goal?

div.head: APPIANI.
div.p: How could you, dear mother, suspect this of your son? But it is true. I am to-day unusually dejected and gloomy. All that I have seen, heard or dreamt, has preached since yesterday, and before yesterday this doctrine to me--to be but one step from the goal, and not to have attained it, is in reality the same. This one idea engrosses all my thoughts. What can it mean? I understand it not.

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: You make me uneasy, Count.

div.head: APPIANI.
div.p: One thought succeeds another. I am vexed--angry with my friends and with myself.

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: Why so?

div.head: APPIANI.
div.p: My friends absolutely require, that, before I solemnize my marriage, I should acquaint the Prince with my intentions. They allow I am not bound to do this, but maintain that respect towards him demands it; and I have been weak enough to consent. I have already ordered my carriage for the purpose.

div.head: CLAUDIA (starts).
div.p: To wait upon the Prince!
Pirro, afterwards Marinelli, Count Appiani, Claudia.
Enter Pirro.

div.head: PIRRO.
div.p: My lady, the Marquis Marinelli is at the door, and inquires for the Count.

div.head: APPIANI.
div.p: For me!

div.head: PIRRO.
div.p: Here his lordship comes. (Opens the door and exit.)
Enter Marinelli.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: I ask pardon, madam. My lord Count, I called at your house, and was informed that I should find you here. I have important business with you. Once more pardon, madam. It will occupy but a few minutes.

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: I will not impede it. (Curtseys and exit.)
Marinelli, Appiani.

div.head: APPIANI.
div.p: Now, my lord?

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: I come from his Highness.

div.head: APPIANI.
div.p: What are his commands?

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: I am proud to be the bearer of this distinguished favour; and if Count Appiani will not wilfully misunderstand one of his most devoted friends----

div.head: APPIANI.
div.p: Proceed, I pray, without more ceremony.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: I will. The Prince is obliged to send an ambassador immediately to the Duke of Massa respecting his marriage with the Princess his daughter. He was long undetermined whom to appoint, till his choice at last has fallen upon you, my lord.

div.head: APPIANI.
div.p: Upon me?

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: Yes--and if friendship may be allowed to boast, I was instrumental----

div.head: APPIANI.
div.p: Truly I am at a loss for thanks. I had long renounced the hope of being noticed by the Prince.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: I am sure he only waited for a proper opportunity, and if the present mission be not sufficiently worthy of Count Appiani, I own my friendship has been too precipitate.

div.head: APPIANI.
div.p: Friendship, friendship! every third word. With whom am I speaking? The Marquis Marinelli's friendship I never dreamt of gaining.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: I acknowledge my fault, Count Appiani, my unpardonable fault in wishing to be your friend without your permission. But what of that? The favour of his Highness, and the dignity he offers, remain the same. I do not doubt you will accept them with pleasure.

div.head: APPIANI (after some consideration).
div.p: Undoubtedly.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: Come, then, with me.

div.head: APPIANI.
div.p: Whither?

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: To the Prince's palace at Dosalo. All is ready. You must depart to-day.

div.head: APPIANI.
div.p: What say you? To-day?

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: Yes. Rather now than an hour hence. The business presses.

div.head: APPIANI.
div.p: Indeed! Then I am sorry I must decline the honour which the Prince intended to confer upon me.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: How?

div.head: APPIANI.
div.p: I cannot depart to-day,--nor to-morrow--nor the next day.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: You are jesting, Count.

div.head: APPIANI.
div.p: With you?

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: Incomparable! If with the Prince, the joke is so much the merrier.--You cannot?

div.head: APPIANI.
div.p: No, my lord, no--and I trust that the Prince himself will think my excuse sufficient.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: I am eager to hear it.

div.head: APPIANI.
div.p: Oh, it is a mere trifle. I mean to be married to-day.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: Indeed!--and what then?

div.head: APPIANI.
div.p: And what then?--Your question shows a cursed simplicity!

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: There are examples, Count, of marriages having been deferred. I do not mean to infer that the delay was pleasant to the bride and bridegroom. To them it was, no doubt, a trial, yet the sovereign's command----

div.head: APPIANI.
div.p: Sovereign's command? A sovereign of my own option, I am not so strictly bound to obey. I admit that you owe the Prince absolute obedience, but not I. I came to his court a volunteer. I wished to enjoy the honour of serving him, but not of being his slave. I am the vassal of a greater sovereign.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: Greater or smaller, a monarch is a monarch.

div.head: APPIANI.
div.p: Idle controversy! Enough! Tell the Prince what you have heard. Tell him I am sorry I cannot accept the honour, as I to-day intend to solemnize an union which will consummate my happiness.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: Will you not at the same time inform him with whom?

div.head: APPIANI.
div.p: With Emilia Galotti.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: The daughter of this family?

div.head: APPIANI.
div.p: Yes.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: Humph!

div.head: APPIANI.
div.p: What do you mean?

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: I mean that there would be the less difficulty in deferring the ceremony till your return.

div.head: APPIANI.
div.p: The ceremony?

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: Yes. The worthy parents will not think much about it.

div.head: APPIANI.
div.p: The worthy parents?

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: And Emilia will remain faithful to you, of course.

div.head: APPIANI.
div.p: Of course?----You are an impertinent ape, with your "of course."

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: This to me, Count?

div.head: APPIANI.
div.p: Why not?

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: Heaven and hell! You shall hear from me.

div.head: APPIANI.
div.p: Pshaw! The ape is malicious, but----

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: Death and damnation!--Count, I demand satisfaction.

div.head: APPIANI.
div.p: You shall have it.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: ----And would insist upon it instantly--but that I should not like to spoil the day for the loving bridegroom.

div.head: APPIANI.
div.p: Good--natured creature!--(seizes his arm). I own an embassy to Massa does not suit me, but still I have time enough to take a walk with you. Come.

div.head: MARINELLI (extricates himself from the Count's grasp).
div.p: Patience, my lord, patience! (Exit.)
Appiani, Claudia.

div.head: APPIANI.
div.p: Go, worthless wretch----Ha! that does me good. My blood circulates----I feel different and all the better.

div.head: CLAUDIA (hastily and alarmed).
div.p: Heavens! My lord--I overheard an angry altercation. Your cheek is flushed. What has happened?

div.head: APPIANI.
div.p: Nothing, Madam, nothing. The chamberlain Marinelli has conferred a favour on me. He has saved me a visit to the Prince.

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: Indeed!

div.head: APPIANI.
div.p: We can therefore leave town earlier. I go to give orders to my people, and shall return immediately. Emilia will, in the meantime, get ready.

div.head: CLAUDIA.
div.p: May I feel quite at ease, my lord?

div.head: APPIANI.
div.p: Perfectly so, dear Madam. (Exeunt severally.)
Scene, an apartment in the Prince's country palace.
Enter Prince and Marinelli.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: In vain. He refused the proffered honour with the greatest contempt.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: This ends all hope, then. Things take their course,

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: According to all appearances.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: I relied so firmly on your project--but who knows how ridiculously you acted? I ought to have recollected that though a blockhead's counsel may be good, it requires a clever man to execute it.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: A pretty reward, this!

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: Why should you be rewarded?

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: For having risked my life on the venture. Finding that neither raillery nor reason could induce the Count to sacrifice his love to honour, I tried to rouse his anger. I said things to him which made him forget himself. He used insulting expressions, and I demanded satisfaction--yes, satisfaction on the spot. One of us must fall, thought I. Should it be his fate, the field is ours--should it be mine--why, he must fly, and the Prince will at least gain time.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: Did you act thus, Marinelli?

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: Yes; he, who is ready to sacrifice his life for princes, ought to learn beforehand how grateful they are likely to be.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: And the Count? Report says that he is not the man to wait till satisfaction is a second time demanded.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: No doubt, in ordinary cases. Who can blame him? He said that he had then something of greater consequence than a duel to occupy his thoughts, and put me off till a week after his marriage.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: With Emilia Galotti. The idea drives me to distraction----Thus, then, the affair ended, and now you come hither to boast that you risked your life in my behalf--sacrificed yourself for me.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: What more, my lord, would you have had me do?

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: More? As if you had done anything!

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: May I be allowed to ask what your Highness has done for yourself? You were so fortunate as to see her at church. What is the result of your conference?

div.head: PRINCE (with a sneer).
div.p: You have curiosity enough--but I will satisfy it. All happened as I wished. You need take no further trouble, my most serviceable friend. She met my proposal more than half way. I ought to have taken her with me instantly. (In a cold and commanding tone.) Now you have heard what you wished to know, and may depart.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: And may depart! Yes, yes. Thus the song ends, and so 'twould be were I to attempt the impossible. The impossible, did I say? No. Impossible it is not--only a daring attempt. Had we the girl in our power, I would answer for it that no marriage should take place.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: Ay--you would answer for anything. I suppose, for instance, you would like to take a troop of my guards, lie in ambush by the highway, fall to the number of fifty upon one carriage, and bear the girl in triumph to me.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: A girl has been carried off before now by force, though there has been no appearance of force in the transaction.----

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: If you were able to do this, you would not talk so much about it.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: ----But I cannot be answerable for the consequences. Unforeseen accidents may happen.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: Is it my custom to make people answerable for what they cannot help?

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: Therefore your Highness will--(a pistol is fired at a distance). Ha! What was that? Did not my ears deceive me? Did not your Highness also hear a shot. And hark! Another!

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: What means this? What is the matter?

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: How if I were more active than you deemed me?

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: More active! Explain, then----

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: In short, what I mentioned is now taking place.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: Is it possible?

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: But forget not, Prince, what you just now promised. You pledge your word that----

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: The necessary precautions I hope have been taken.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: Yes, as carefully as possible. The execution of my plan is entrusted to people on whom I can rely. The road, as you know, runs close by your park fence. There the carriage will be attacked by a party, apparently to rob the travellers. Another band (one of whom is my trusty servant) will rush from the park as if to assist those who are attacked. During the sham battle between the two parties, my servant will seize Emilia, as if to rescue her, and bring her through the park into the palace. This is the plan. What says your Highness now?

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: You surprise me beyond measure. A fearful anxiety comes o'er me. (Marinelli walks to the window.) What are you looking at?

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: That must be the scene of action--yes, and see, some one in a mask has just leapt over the fence--doubtless to acquaint me with the result. Withdraw awhile, your Highness.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: Ah, Marinelli----

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: Well--now, doubtless, I have done too much--as I before had done too little.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: Not so--not so--yet I cannot perceive----

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: Perceive?--It is best done at one blow. Withdraw quickly. You must not be seen here.
(Exit Prince.)
Marinelli and presently Angelo.

div.head: MARINELLI (goes again to the window).
div.p: The carriage is returning slowly to town. So slowly? and at each door a servant? These appearances do not please me; they show the plot has only half succeeded. They are driving some wounded person carefully, and he is not dead. The fellow in the mask comes nearer. 'Tis Angelo himself--foolhardy! But he knows the windings of this place. He beckons to me--he must know that he has succeeded.--Ha! ha! Count Appiani. You, who refused an embassy to Massa, have been obliged to go a longer journey. Who taught you to recognize apes so well? 'Tis true, they are malicious (walks towards the door). Well, Angelo?
Enter Angelo, with his mash in his hand.

div.head: ANGELO.
div.p: Be ready, my lord. She will be here directly.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: How did you succeed in other respects?

div.head: ANGELO.
div.p: As you wished, I have no doubt.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: How is it with the Count?

div.head: ANGELO.
div.p: So, so. But he must have had some suspicions, for he was not quite unprepared.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: Quick, tell me--is he dead?

div.head: ANGELO.
div.p: I am sorry for him, poor man.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: There! Take that for thy compassion (gives him a purse).

div.head: ANGELO.
div.p: And our poor Nicolo too, he has shared the same luck.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: What! Loss on both sides?

div.head: ANGELO.
div.p: Yes. I could cry for the honest lad's fate; though I come in for another quarter of this purse by it; for I am his heir, since I avenged him. This is a law among us, and as good a law, methinks, as ever was made for the support of friendship and fidelity. This Nicolo, my lord----

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: No more of your Nicolo! The Count----

div.head: ANGELO.
div.p: Zounds! The Count finished him, and I finished the Count. He fell, and though he might be alive when they put him into the coach, I'll answer for it that he will never come alive out of it.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: Were you but sure of this, Angelo----

div.head: ANGELO.
div.p: I'll forfeit your custom, if it be not true. Have you any further commands? For I have a long journey. We must be across the frontier before sunset.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: Go, then.

div.head: ANGELO.
div.p: Should anything else occur in my way, you know where to inquire for me. What any other can venture to do will be no magic for me, and my terms are lower than any other's. (Exit.)

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: 'Tis well--yet not so well as it might have been. Shame on thee, Angelo, to be such a niggard! Surely the Count was worthy of a second shot. Now, he may die in agony; poor Count! Shame, Angelo! It was a cruel and bungling piece of work. The Prince must not know what has happened. He himself must discover how advantageous this death is to him. Death! What would I not give to be certain of it!
The Prince, Marinelli.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: Here she comes up the avenue. She flies before the servants. Fear gives wings to her feet. She must not suspect our design. She thinks she is escaping from robbers. How long will her mistake last?

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: At least we have her here.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: But will not her mother come in search of her? Will not the Count follow her? What can we do then? How can I keep her from them?

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: To all this I confess I can make no reply. But we must see. Compose yourself, Prince. This first step was, at all events, necessary.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: How so, if we are obliged to recede?

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: But perhaps we need not. There are a thousand things on which we may make further steps. Have you forgotten the chief one?

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: How can I have forgotten that of which I never thought? What mean you by the chief one?

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: The art of pleasing and persuading--which in a prince who loves can never fail.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: Can never fail! True, except when it is most needed. I have already made a poor attempt in this art to-day. All my flattery, all my entreaties could not extract one word from her. Mute, trembling, and abashed, she stood before me like a criminal who fears the judge's fatal sentence. Her terror was infectious. I trembled also and concluded by imploring her forgiveness. Scarcely dare I speak to her again--and, at all events, I dare not be present when she arrives. You, Marinelli, must receive her. I will listen to your conversation, and join you when I am more collected.
Marinelli, presently his servant Battista, and Emilia.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: If she did not see him fall--and of course she could not, as she fled instantly But she comes, and I too do not wish to be the first to meet her eye (withdraws to a corner of the apartment).
Enter Battista and Emilia.

div.head: BATTISTA.
div.p: This way--this way--dear lady.

div.head: EMILIA (out of breath).
div.p: Oh! I thank you, my friend--I thank you. But, Heavens! Where am I? Quite alone, too! Where are my mother, and the Count? They are surely coming? Are they not close behind me?

div.head: BATTISTA.
div.p: I suppose so.

div.head: EMILIA.
div.p: You suppose so? Are you not certain? Have you not seen them? Were not pistols fired behind us?

div.head: BATTISTA.
div.p: Pistols? Was it so?

div.head: EMILIA.
div.p: Surely. Oh, Heavens! and the Count or my mother is shot.

div.head: BATTISTA.
div.p: I'll go in search of them instantly.

div.head: EMILIA.
div.p: Not without me! I'll go with you! I must go with you. Come, my friend.

div.head: MARINELLI (approaches as if he had just entered).
div.p: Ha! fair lady! What misfortune, or rather what good fortune--what fortunate misfortune has procured us the honour----

div.head: EMILIA (astonished).
div.p: How!--You here, my lord!--This then is doubtless your house. Pardon my intrusion. We have been attacked by robbers. Some good people came to our assistance,--and this honest man took me out of the carriage and conducted me hither. But I am alarmed to find that I alone am rescued. My mother must be still in danger. I heard pistols fired behind us. Perhaps she is dead,--and yet I live. Pardon me. I must away, I must return to the place, which I ought not to have left.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: Compose yourself, dear lady. All is well. The beloved persons, for whom you feel this tender anxiety, will soon be here.--Run, Battista; they may perhaps not know where the lady is. See whether you can find them in any of the lodges, and conduct them hither instantly.
(Exit Battista.)

div.head: EMILIA.
div.p: Are you sure they are all safe? Has nothing happened to them?--Oh, what a day of terrors has this been to me! But I ought not to remain here; I should hasten to meet them.

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: Why so, dear lady? You are already breathless and exhausted. Compose yourself, and condescend to step into this room, where you will find better accommodation than here. I feel certain that the Prince has already found your gracious mother, and is escorting her hither.

div.head: EMILIA.
div.p: Who do you say?

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: Our gracious Prince himself.

div.head: EMILIA (extremely terrified).
div.p: The Prince!

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: He flew to your assistance at the first intelligence. He is highly incensed that such a crime should have been committed so near to his villa, nay, almost before his eyes. He has sent in search of the villains, and if they be seized, their punishment will be most severe.

div.head: EMILIA.
div.p: The Prince!--Where am I then?

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: At Dosalo, the Prince's villa.

div.head: EMILIA.
div.p: How strange!--And you think he will soon arrive?--But with my mother too?

div.head: MARINELLI.
div.p: Here he is, already.
The Prince, Emilia, and Marinellies.

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: Where is she? Where is she?--We have sought you everywhere, dear lady.--You are well, I hope? Now, all is well. The Count and your mother----

div.head: EMILIA.
div.p: Oh, your Highness! Where are they? Where is my mother?

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: Not far off, close at hand.

div.head: EMILIA.
div.p: Heavens! In what a situation shall I perhaps find one or other of them! For your Highness conceals from me--I perceive----

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: I conceal nothing, be assured. Lean on my arm, and accompany me to them without fear.

div.head: EMILIA (irresolute).
div.p: But--if they be not wounded--if my suspicions be not true--why are they not already here?

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: Hasten then, that all these sad apprehensions may at once be banished.

div.head: EMILIA.
div.p: What shall I do? (wrings her hands).

div.head: PRINCE.
div.p: How, dear lady! Can you harbour any suspicion against me?

div.head: EMILIA (falls at his feet).
div.p: On my knees I entreat you----

div.head: PRINCE (raising her).
div.p: I am quite ashamed.--Yes, Emilia, I deserve this mute reproach. My conduct this morning cannot be justified, or even excused. Pardon my weakness: I ought not to have made you uneasy by an avowal, from which I could expect no advantage. I was amply punished by the speechless agitation with which you listened to it, or rather did not listen to it. And if I might be allowed to think this accident the signal of more favourable fortune--the most wondrous respite of my final sentence--this accident, which allows me to behold and speak to you again before my hopes for ever vanish--this accident, which gives me an opportunity of imploring your forgiveness--yet will I--do not tremble--yet will I rely only and entirely on your looks. Not a sigh, not a syllable shall offend you. Only wound me not with suspicions--do not for a moment doubt the unbounded influence which you possess over me--only imagine not that you need any protection against me. And now come--come where delights more in harmony with your feelings, await you. (Leads her away, not without opposition.) Follow us, Marinelli.
(Exeunt Prince and Emilia.)

div.head: MARINELLI.
